entities.summary: Eardwulf of Kent, King of Kent (765 CE), played a pivotal role in the medieval period. He was one of the five kings of Kent, a region in southern England, who jointly ruled with Æðelberht II. Eardwulf's reign was marked by the transition from Paganism to Christianity, with the conversion of the Kingdom of Kent. This event had significant repercussions, shaping the religious landscape of England and influencing the trajectory of the Anglo-Saxon Kingdoms. Eardwulf's legacy is tied to the establishment of the Church of England, with his successor, Æthelberht's son, succeeding him in the role of king of Kent. The conversion of Kent also had far-reaching consequences, contributing to the eventual Christianization of England and the decline of Paganism. Eardwulf's impact can be seen in the development of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, a collection of annals that recorded the history of England from the 5th to the 11th centuries. The king's reign also saw the rise of the Kentish dynasty, which would go on to shape the political landscape of England for centuries to come. Eardwulf's significance can be measured by the enduring legacy of the Church of England, which continues to play a vital role in the country's spiritual life. The conversion of Kent, however, also had a darker side, as it contributed to the displacement of the native pagan population, leaving a lasting impact on the cultural and social fabric of England.
